query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion, the coupled degradation is governed by a dynamic interplay wherein tribological wear continuously removes the protective passive oxide film faster than it can reform. This constant removal exposes fresh metal that corrodes more aggressively, while the ensuing corrosion further disrupts the film structure, reducing its ability to protect against wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, passivating high-entropy alloy that naturally develops a protective oxide layer in ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to sliding wear under a controlled corrosive (aqueous, pH-controlled) environment versus a matched inert (non-corrosive) environment.
generation.conditions: Controlled laboratory conditions with identical mechanical loading, sliding speed, temperature, and humidity; the only difference is the electrochemical environment (corrosive electrolyte vs. inert medium).
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and kinetics of the passive oxide film at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically disrupts and removes the protective oxide film. When the rate of film removal exceeds the alloy’s repassivation rate, the continuously exposed substrate undergoes accelerated corrosion. This corrosion damage, in turn, undermines the mechanical properties of the near-surface region, accelerating wear in a synergistic cycle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline of wear-only (in an inert environment) or corrosion-only conditions, the combined tribo-corrosion will lead to a total degradation that exceeds the sum of its individual parts. Specifically, higher material loss (measured by mass loss or volume loss), increased localized pit formation, and more extensive surface damage will be observed under tribo-corrosion conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of the alloy under similar wear conditions in an inert medium where no significant corrosion occurs, and, separately, under static corrosion conditions without mechanical wear.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold when the alloy’s repassivation kinetics are insufficient to keep pace with the wear-induced film removal. If, however, the alloy has rapid reformation of the passive film or if the wear rate is very low, the coupling effect could be minimized and the predicted synergistic degradation might not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the synergistic effect is uncertain, as it may depend on alloy composition-specific repassivation kinetics, local variations in wear intensity, and corrosive severity. The influence of microstructural features (e.g., grain boundary distribution) on passive film stability under wear is also not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled sliding tribometer experiment in two conditions: one set under a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., chloride-containing solution with controlled pH) and one set under an inert medium (e.g., deionized water or air). In addition, include a static corrosion test without wear for comparison. Monitor the evolution of surface film integrity, wear track morphology, and electrochemical behavior using in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
measurements: Mass loss or wear track volume quantification
Surface imaging (SEM/AFM) to assess film integrity and pitting
Electrochemical measurements (EIS, potentiodynamic polarization) to track corrosion kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined tribo-corrosion condition does not exhibit a degradation (in terms of material loss, pitting density, or both) that is significantly greater than the sum of individual wear-only and corrosion-only conditions, then the hypothesis that the dynamic interplay between film removal and insufficient repassivation drives the enhanced degradation would be falsified.
